questions.stem: How does memory differ from learning?
options: Memory happens consciously, while learning is always unconscious
Learning is acquiring new information; memory is retaining it over time
Memory is acquiring new information; learning is retaining it over time
Learning involves only skills, while memory involves only facts
questions.explanation: Learning is a relatively lasting change from experience, and memory is the retention and later retrieval of what was learned. The two are closely linked: without memory, learning could not be shown.

questions.stem: A student hears a new word, stores it and recalls it a week later in an essay. Recalling it is an example of:
options: storage
consolidation
retrieval
encoding
questions.explanation: Encoding converts information into a form that can be stored, storage keeps it over time, and retrieval brings it back into awareness when needed.

questions.stem: A student reads a textbook page while thinking about the weekend and later remembers nothing from it. Which memory process most likely failed?
options: encoding
retrieval
decay
consolidation
questions.explanation: If attention is elsewhere, information is not processed into a form that can be stored, so it never enters long-term memory. This is an encoding failure rather than a retrieval problem.

questions.stem: In the modal model of memory, which store has a very large capacity but holds information for only a fraction of a second to a few seconds?
options: long-term memory
working long-term memory
the sensory register
short-term memory
questions.explanation: The sensory register briefly holds a great deal of incoming sensory information: visual images for a fraction of a second and sounds for a few seconds. Only information that is attended to passes to short-term memory.

questions.stem: Which description of short-term memory is most accurate?
options: an unlimited number of items, lasting only a fraction of a second
about 7 plus or minus 2 items, lasting several hours without rehearsal
about 7 plus or minus 2 items, lasting up to about 30 seconds without rehearsal
an unlimited number of items, lasting a lifetime without any rehearsal
questions.explanation: Short-term memory holds a small amount of information, often given as about seven items, for up to about 18 to 30 seconds unless it is rehearsed. Long-term memory has unlimited capacity and duration.

questions.stem: Which is a weakness of the modal model of memory?
options: It proposes that memory has more than one store
It is supported by evidence such as the serial position effect
It distinguishes stores by their capacity and duration
It presents short-term memory as a single, simple store
questions.explanation: Later research suggests short-term memory involves several components working together, and that information does not always need rehearsal to reach long-term memory. Evidence such as the serial position effect is a strength of the model.

questions.stem: A patient can recall events from before a brain injury but cannot form new long-term memories, although he can hold a phone number in mind for a few seconds. How does this support the modal model?
options: It suggests the sensory register stores memories permanently
It shows that long-term memory has a capacity of about seven items
It shows that all memory depends on a single unified store
It suggests short-term and long-term memory are separate stores
questions.explanation: His short-term memory works, and old long-term memories remain, but information cannot be transferred into long-term storage. This pattern fits the idea of separate stores, as in cases such as Henry Molaison.

questions.stem: Remembering how to ride a bike is an example of:
options: episodic memory
semantic memory
sensory memory
procedural memory
questions.explanation: Procedural memory stores skills and how to perform actions. Episodic memory stores personal events, and semantic memory stores facts and general knowledge.

questions.stem: Remembering your tenth birthday party is episodic memory, while knowing that Adelaide is the capital of South Australia is semantic memory. What is the key difference?
options: Episodic memories are implicit; semantic memories are always implicit too
Episodic memories last seconds; semantic memories last a lifetime
Episodic memories are personal events; semantic memories are general facts
Episodic memories are skills; semantic memories are personal events
questions.explanation: Episodic memory holds events a person experienced, tied to a time and place. Semantic memory holds facts and knowledge, without needing to recall when they were learned.

questions.stem: Which type of memory is usually implicit?
options: procedural memory
episodic memory
semantic memory
short-term memory
questions.explanation: Procedural memories, such as typing or tying shoelaces, are retrieved without conscious effort, so they are implicit. Episodic and semantic memories are explicit because they are recalled consciously.

questions.stem: An experienced typist can type a sentence quickly without looking but struggles to name the letters on the top row of the keyboard. What does this show?
options: Typing skill is stored in the sensory register rather than long-term memory
The typist's episodic memory has decayed through lack of use
Implicit procedural memory can work without explicit recall of it
Explicit semantic memory controls typing better than procedural memory does
questions.explanation: The typing skill is procedural and retrieved automatically, but naming letter positions requires explicit, conscious recall, which the typist has never needed to practise.

questions.stem: According to the levels of processing model, which task would lead to the best recall of a list of words?
options: deciding whether each word fits into a sentence
deciding whether each word is in capital letters
deciding whether each word rhymes with 'cat'
counting the number of letters in each word
questions.explanation: Deep, semantic processing of meaning produces stronger memory than shallow processing of appearance or sound. Fitting a word into a sentence requires thinking about its meaning.

questions.stem: Which study technique uses deep processing?
options: putting a concept into your own words
reading the textbook page aloud
highlighting key words in a colour
copying the notes out word for word
questions.explanation: Reworking information in your own words, linking it to what you already know or explaining it to someone requires thinking about meaning, which is deep processing. Copying and reading aloud are shallow.

questions.stem: According to displacement theory, information is forgotten from short-term memory because:
options: information cannot be found because the right cue is missing
information was not given enough time to become stable
new information pushes out old once capacity is full
old information gradually fades through lack of use over years
questions.explanation: Short-term memory has limited capacity, so new items replace older ones. Fading through disuse is decay, missing cues is retrieval failure, and instability is lack of consolidation.

questions.stem: Participants hear a list of 20 words and recall them immediately, remembering the first and last words best. When recall is delayed by 30 seconds of counting, the advantage for the last words disappears. Why?
options: The first words were in short-term memory and were displaced by the counting
The last words had decayed from long-term memory during the 30 seconds
The counting acted as a retrieval cue for the first words in the list
The last words were in short-term memory and were displaced by the counting
questions.explanation: The recency effect reflects items still in short-term memory. Counting displaces them, so recency disappears, while the primacy effect remains because early words were rehearsed into long-term memory.

questions.stem: A student who has learned Spanish this year keeps using Spanish words when trying to speak the French she learned last year. This is an example of:
options: retroactive interference
proactive interference
decay
lack of consolidation
questions.explanation: In retroactive interference, new learning disrupts the recall of older information. Proactive interference is when old learning disrupts new information.

questions.stem: After moving house, a person keeps writing her old address on forms. This is an example of:
options: decay
proactive interference
retroactive interference
displacement
questions.explanation: The older, well-learned address interferes with recalling the new one, which is proactive interference. Interference is most likely when the two pieces of information are similar.

questions.stem: A person cannot recall a classmate's name at a party, but remembers it instantly when someone mentions the school they attended. Which theory explains the forgetting?
options: lack of consolidation
retrieval failure
decay
displacement
questions.explanation: The name was stored but could not be accessed without a suitable cue. When the cue was provided, retrieval succeeded, so the forgetting was due to retrieval failure.

questions.stem: Divers learned word lists either underwater or on land and recalled them in the same or the other setting. Recall was better in the same setting. Which explanation fits?
options: new lists displace older lists in long-term memory
context cues present at encoding aid retrieval
memories decay faster on land than underwater
learning underwater causes lack of consolidation
questions.explanation: This study, by Godden and Baddeley, showed context-dependent memory: features of the environment at encoding act as retrieval cues. Without them, retrieval failure is more likely.

questions.stem: According to decay theory, forgetting from long-term memory occurs because:
options: new memories interfere with older, similar memories
the cues needed to find the memory are not present
the brain was disrupted while the memory was forming
memory traces fade over time if they are not used
questions.explanation: Decay theory proposes that unused memory traces gradually weaken and fade. A weakness is that some old, unused memories are recalled well, suggesting decay cannot explain all forgetting.

questions.stem: A footballer who is knocked unconscious cannot remember the few minutes before the collision, though he remembers earlier events. Which theory best explains this?
options: decay
lack of consolidation
proactive interference
retrieval failure
questions.explanation: New memories need time to be consolidated into a stable long-term form. The injury disrupted this process, so the most recent memories were lost while older, consolidated ones remained.

questions.stem: How do memory problems in Alzheimer's disease typically change over time?
options: Recent memories are affected first, then older memories and skills
Older memories are lost first, while recent memories remain clear
Procedural skills are lost first, while all facts remain intact
Memory problems appear suddenly and then stay the same for life
questions.explanation: Alzheimer's disease is progressive. Difficulty forming new memories usually appears early, and as the disease advances, older memories, knowledge and eventually everyday skills are lost.

questions.stem: Which explanation of memory problems in Alzheimer's disease is most accurate?
options: A single large stroke destroys the whole cortex at one time
The sensory register stops working, so no information is taken in
Memories are stored in the wrong order and cannot be retrieved
Plaques and tangles damage neurons, early on in the hippocampus
questions.explanation: Alzheimer's disease involves beta-amyloid plaques and tau tangles that disrupt and kill neurons. The hippocampus, important for forming new memories, is affected early, which explains early problems with new learning.

questions.stem: In many cultures, oral traditions pass on laws, histories and practices across generations. What does this show about memory?
options: Culture influences what is remembered and how it is learned
Memory works identically in every culture regardless of practices
Information passed on by speech is always forgotten quickly
Only written information can be stored in long-term memory
questions.explanation: Cultural practices, such as storytelling and yarning in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander cultures, shape what people value remembering and the techniques used to remember it.

questions.stem: Why might a researcher use an observational design or focus groups to study cultural differences in memory, rather than a laboratory experiment?
options: They allow the researcher to prove which culture has the better memory
They control every extraneous variable more tightly than experiments do
They produce only numerical data, which is easier to compare
Memory can be studied in real settings and in people's own terms
questions.explanation: Laboratory tasks may be unfamiliar or culturally biased. Observation and focus groups capture memory as it is used in real contexts and let participants explain practices themselves, though they give less control and are harder to generalise.

questions.stem: Which is a disadvantage of using focus groups to research how culture influences memory?
options: Focus groups require a laboratory setting to work
Dominant members may influence what others say
Focus groups cannot collect any qualitative data
Participants are never able to explain their views
questions.explanation: Focus groups give rich qualitative data, but group dynamics can lead some members to conform or stay quiet, and findings may be hard to generalise.

questions.stem: A student remembers the planets using the sentence 'My Very Easy Method Just Speeds Up Naming'. This mnemonic is an example of:
options: an acrostic
the method of loci
over-learning
distributed practice
questions.explanation: An acrostic uses the first letter of each word in a sentence to stand for items to be recalled. The method of loci links items to places along a familiar route.

questions.stem: Two students each study for six hours. One studies in a single session the night before the test; the other studies one hour a day for six days. Who is likely to remember more, and why?
options: both equally, because the total study time is the same
the first student, because over-learning occurs in long sessions
the second student, because distributed practice improves retention
the first student, because massed practice keeps the material fresh
questions.explanation: Distributed practice, spacing study over time, produces better long-term retention than massed practice, or cramming, even when total time is equal.

questions.stem: Over-learning means:
options: learning so much at once that memory becomes overloaded
learning material that is beyond what the test requires
studying the same material in many different rooms
continuing to practise after material has been mastered
questions.explanation: Practising beyond the point of first mastery strengthens memory and makes it more resistant to forgetting, for example under stress in an exam.

questions.stem: Researchers have tested electrical stimulation through electrodes implanted in the brain to improve memory. Which is the main disadvantage of this technique compared with transcranial magnetic stimulation?
options: It can only be used on people who have no memory problems
It works only on short-term memory and never on long-term memory
It must be applied by holding a coil against the scalp
It requires brain surgery, with risks such as infection
questions.explanation: Implanted electrodes allow precise stimulation of deep brain areas, but they need invasive surgery. TMS uses a magnetic coil held over the scalp, so it is non-invasive, though its effects are usually temporary.

questions.stem: How does transcranial magnetic stimulation work?
options: Sound waves are directed at the ears to strengthen memories
A magnetic coil over the scalp induces activity in the brain
Electrodes are surgically implanted to stimulate deep brain areas
A drug is injected to increase acetylcholine in the hippocampus
questions.explanation: TMS uses a rapidly changing magnetic field from a coil on the scalp to stimulate neurons in the cortex below. It is non-invasive but mainly reaches areas near the surface of the brain.

questions.stem: Witnesses to a car crash video were asked how fast the cars were going when they 'smashed' into each other, or when they 'hit' each other. The 'smashed' group gave higher estimates. This shows the effect of:
options: leading questions
selective attention
context cues
displacement
questions.explanation: In Loftus and Palmer's 1974 study, the wording of the question altered what witnesses reported. Leading questions can distort memory and lead to inaccurate testimony.

questions.stem: A witness to a robbery remembers the robber's gun in detail but cannot describe the robber's face. Which factor best explains this?
options: a schema for typical robberies
proactive interference
decay of the memory trace
selective attention to the weapon
questions.explanation: Attention is limited, and a threatening object such as a weapon can draw it away from other details, such as the face. Unattended details are not encoded.

questions.stem: A witness says the robber wore a balaclava, though the robber did not. The witness's idea of a typical robber may have filled the gap. Which factor is this?
options: a schema influencing reconstruction
a leading question from police
selective attention to a weapon
a fair, blind line-up
questions.explanation: Schemas are organised knowledge about what is typical. When memory is incomplete, people reconstruct events using schemas, which can add details that were not there.

questions.stem: A detective believes a suspect is guilty and pays more attention to witness statements that support this. This is an example of:
options: context-dependent memory
retroactive interference
confirmation bias
a cognitive interview
questions.explanation: Confirmation bias is the tendency to seek and favour information that supports existing beliefs, which can lead investigations and testimony towards the wrong person.

questions.stem: Why is it important for the person running a line-up to be 'blind' to which member is the suspect?
options: so the witness feels much more confident when making a choice
so the suspect can stand out clearly from the other people
so the witness is reminded of the original context of the crime
so they cannot unintentionally cue the witness towards the suspect
questions.explanation: An officer who knows the suspect may give subtle verbal or non-verbal cues that influence the witness. A blind administrator removes this source of bias.

questions.stem: In a fair line-up, the suspect should not stand out from the other members. How is this best achieved?
options: the suspect stands in the centre of the line-up every time
all members match the witness's description of the offender
the suspect is the only person wearing similar clothing
the other members are clearly older or younger than the suspect
questions.explanation: If the suspect is the only person who fits the description, the witness may choose them by elimination rather than recognition. Fillers should be similar to the description so the choice relies on memory.

questions.stem: Which technique is part of a cognitive interview?
options: asking the witness to mentally reinstate the scene and report everything
asking the witness short, direct questions that suggest the answers
showing the witness photos of the suspect before the interview begins
asking the witness to report only details they are certain about
questions.explanation: Cognitive interviews use context reinstatement, reporting everything however trivial, recalling events in different orders and from different perspectives. These provide more retrieval cues and increase accurate recall without leading the witness.
